name: Carla Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining firms or technology companies, and what you tell me stays confidential. What is an ordinary shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck crew and keep a paper list of route hazards in the cab. I check the road and radio calls myself, then walk the newer operators through the loading area before the first run.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about that work, and what gets under your skin?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing everyone finish a shift safely and knowing my crew took the time to do it right. The pay is high for this job, and I have more than six months saved, but I do not like decisions being made over our heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a tool tidied the routine notices, it would not change the important part of the shift for me. I would still walk the route and check the radio before I sent a truck down the haul road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that small time savings are fine if nobody drops the safety checks. I would also say there is no need to buy every new system when a paper hazard list already works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job and pay look secure in this mild picture, and I have a good cushion if a shift gets cancelled. I am not going to change a safe routine just to keep up with a tool that saves a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my haul-truck rotation and compare any new notice with the paper hazard list. I would continue putting my overtime into savings and keep the same amount for the monthly union dues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my income and my work in this version. If a little automation helps the crew without changing how we do safety checks, I can let it sit in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you object to the new notice system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it left out a radio closure or put a hazard in the wrong place, I would ask the foreman to suspend that feature. I would want the safety delegate, Rafi, to review the mistake with the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test the tool yourself, or wait for the safety delegate to decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the output, but I would not ask it to choose a route for me. If Rafi and the operators agreed the notices were accurate, I would let the clerks use it for routine sorting.

say: I would allow small savings only if **safety checks stay**.
I would keep the paper list if it already **works**.
think: I think my job and pay look **secure** in this picture.
My cushion lets me **ignore a needless upgrade**.
do: Keep my **haul-truck rotation** and compare notices with the hazard list.
Continue overtime savings and pay the **union dues**.
feel: I feel **calm** about income and work in this mild picture.
S0.quote: I would still walk the route and check the radio before I sent a truck down the haul road.
fieldNote: Carla trusts **field checks** over a small automation change.
Her **strong savings** and high pay make the baseline work feel secure.
She would involve the **safety delegate** if a notice were wrong.

steps.text: Keep the truck rotation and compare notices with the hazard list
Continue overtime deposits into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may use AI for route plans, shift booking and parts orders before robots reach the haul trucks. My driving is hands-on, but as a lead I also spend time checking those plans and writing the handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say workers should have a say in any software that changes a shift or a safety check. I would also tell people the company must explain whether the lead hours and allowance are changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not expect a desk system to take my truck tomorrow, but I can see the lead paperwork shrinking. I would ask the union to bargain over paid training and hours before the mine changes the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the proposed planner to the union safety meeting and ask who is responsible when a route is wrong. If a change cut my lead hours, I would use my savings to take a paid mechanical inspection course at a nearby mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because my main job still looks safe, but the lead role may lose part of its work. I would not spend my savings on an untested system; I would ask for a written training route first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union safety delegate to raise first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for clear rules on who can override a computer route and how a worker reports a bad recommendation. I would also ask whether the lead allowance stays when the planning work moves to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the system proved accurate on another crew, would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen to the operators who used it and look at their safety record. If the union and the crew could inspect the results, I would consider using the route output as a check, not as the final decision.

say: I would insist workers have a **say in safety software**.
I would ask the company to explain changes to **lead pay**.
think: I do not expect a desk system to take my **truck tomorrow**.
I would ask the union to protect **training and hours**.
do: Bring the planner to the **union safety meeting** and request route oversight.
Take a paid inspection course if lead hours **fall**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because the lead role may shrink, though driving looks safe.
S1.quote: I would say workers should have a say in any software that changes a shift or a safety check.
fieldNote: Carla's concern is the loss of **worker control**, not immediate truck replacement.
She proposes **union bargaining** before the rota changes.
Her savings let her consider a **paid course** without taking on debt.

steps.text: Raise route software and override rules at the union safety meeting
Enroll in a paid mechanical inspection course if lead hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and paperwork could be handled by AGI in 2028, while robots reach the truck work around 2031. I would have five years to prepare for hands-on changes, but the mine might still reduce crews before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI comes first, then robots for hands-on work about three years later. I would ask the mine and union to publish which jobs remain, how many paid training places there are and what the wage will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With high robot exposure, I think my truck job is at real risk by 2031, even if AGI does not drive it first. I have more than six months saved and plenty of other mines nearby, but I do not want to wait until the last year to find a new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the union to secure a paid inspection course, then enroll while I am still on the crew. In 2029, after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection work only if the job description showed physical checks and a wage that matched my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because robots could replace the main task I am paid to do within five years. The savings give me choices, and I would use them to train or move to another mine rather than rely on an aid program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection role is mostly records and scheduling that AGI can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not call it a protected job, because the desk work is exactly what AGI can handle. I would ask whether workers still do physical checks and repairs, and how many positions will remain when robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the mine did not offer paid training this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would raise it through the union and ask nearby mines about their apprenticeship intakes. I can pay for some training myself, but I would want a real employer to confirm the certificate leads to a vacancy.

say: I would say thinking AI comes first and robots follow **three years later**.
I would demand published jobs, **funded training and wages**.
think: I think my truck job is at real risk by **2031**.
I have savings and nearby mines, but I must **move early**.
do: Ask the union to **secure a paid course**, then enroll while staying on the crew.
In 2029, I would apply for **physical inspection work** only with a published wage.
feel: I feel **anxious** because robots could replace my main task within five years.
S2.quote: With high robot exposure, I think my truck job is at real risk by 2031, even if AGI does not drive it first.
fieldNote: Carla recognizes **robot exposure** as the direct threat to her main task.
She has savings and local options, but will not wait until **2031**.
She distinguishes physical inspection from **automatable desk work**.

steps.text: Ask the union to secure a paid inspection course
Enroll in the paid inspection course while remaining on the crew
Apply for physical inspection roles with published wages in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets the union negotiate before the thinking systems arrive, and robots follow about three years after 2031. I would use the lead time to learn physical inspection, but I would not assume those jobs stay once robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the company should start paid apprenticeships now, not after it posts a smaller rota. I would ask the union to secure notice, retraining and fair severance for people whose jobs disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have eight years before robots are expected to do the truck work, which is enough time to build a second skill. The records and planning jobs may go at AGI, so I would focus on physical inspection and ask whether those positions last past 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete a paid heavy equipment inspection course before 2031 and keep my current crew job while I train. In 2032, after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection shifts only if the mine gave me a clear wage and expected duration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the robot date is years away, and I have savings and nearby mines to use. I still want the union to bargain now, since the company might change the crew before the machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in a transition agreement before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want paid training time, a fair notice period and a clear severance formula if my position were removed. I would also want the mine to publish what physical jobs remain once AGI takes the planning work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if the inspection role is a short bridge to the robots, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it if the wage and contract gave me time to look at other mines before 2034. If the hours were too short to cover my costs, I would keep my savings and apply elsewhere rather than treat the role as a permanent answer.

say: I would ask for paid apprenticeships before the **rota shrinks**.
I would bargain for notice, retraining and **fair severance**.
think: I have eight years to build a **second skill** before robots arrive.
I need evidence physical roles last beyond **2034**.
do: Complete a paid **equipment inspection course** before 2031.
In 2032, accept shifts only with a **clear wage and duration**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because the robot date is distant, but the company may change sooner.
S3.quote: I would also want the mine to publish what physical jobs remain once AGI takes the planning work.
fieldNote: Carla sees time to retrain, but wants collective **transition terms** now.
She distinguishes **physical inspection** from thinking tasks AGI can do.
A short bridge role must provide a **wage** and time to move.

steps.text: Bargain through the union for notice and paid training time
Complete the paid equipment inspection course before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives the crew time to plan, and robots are not expected until about three years after the thinking change. I would still ask the mine to tell us how many physical jobs it expects to keep instead of treating that delay as a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union to use the lead time to negotiate paid retraining and a fair transition agreement. I would also say that the company should publish the job numbers before workers have to make a career choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 40 when robots are expected, and my savings and strong pay give me time to move if my truck job changes. I could learn a maintenance trade, but I would ask whether the work still exists after 2039 before I commit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working and take a paid inspection course if it led to a real vacancy. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would review the union's list of physical jobs and compare the pay before changing crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because my job and income look secure for years, and I have time to prepare. I would rather make a move after seeing a funded training route than worry every day about a date more than a decade away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need the union to secure for workers who want to change roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for paid training, public job forecasts and enough notice to finish a course while still earning wages. I would also want workers to have a voice in how the mine decides which physical roles remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2037, if the union list shows few paid jobs beyond 2039, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask other mines about openings and compare them with the maintenance work I had learned. With a strong cushion I can choose carefully, but I would not leave a good wage for an uncertain contract.

say: I would negotiate **paid retraining** and fair transition terms.
I would ask for job numbers before **career choices**.
think: My savings and pay give me **time to move** before the robot shift.
I will check whether maintenance lasts beyond **2039**.
do: Take a paid inspection course tied to a **real vacancy**.
In 2037, compare union job listings and **wages**.
feel: I feel **calm** because work and income look secure for years.
S4.quote: I would rather make a move after seeing a funded training route than worry every day about a date more than a decade away.
fieldNote: Carla views the long lead as **time to negotiate** and prepare.
Her **savings and pay** support choice without assuming a job is guaranteed.
She wants workers to shape decisions about **remaining physical roles**.

steps.text: Negotiate paid inspection training through the union
Review funded training and job numbers before changing roles

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robot lag gives us only until about 2031 before the hands-on task changes. Paid training, a fair transition agreement and real job numbers would help me choose a next step without surrendering worker protections.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A safety decision should not be made by a screen that workers cannot question. I would rather make a move after seeing a funded training route than worry every day about a date more than a decade away.

headlineQuote: A safety decision should not be made by a screen that workers cannot question.
portrait: Carla Mensah is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
She earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of savings or assets.
Plenty of similar local jobs give her **options** if the mine changes.
She distrusts **new technology** and does not use AI tools.
She favors **union bargaining**, paid retraining and a measured individual move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only until about 2031 before robots threaten her hands-on truck work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, fair notice and real job numbers would help Carla choose a next step with worker protections.
